title: Heat Pumps: the Future of Home Heating
summary: Explains the refrigeration cycle, that air conditioners are heat pumps, how cold and defrost reduce performance, backup heat, and why heat pumps beat burning gas on primary energy.

assertions.quote: this heat pump is able to move up to five and a half times as much heat energy as it actually consumes in electricity.
it would need roughly a third the electricity of a plain resistive heater to produce the same amount of heat.

verdicts.note: Resistance heat has a COP of 1 while heat pumps average two to four over a season, so the same heat costs two to four times as much.

assertions.quote: as it gets colder outside, their effectiveness is reduced.
On cold, humid days it has to defrost rather frequently, limiting its output, and reducing efficiency.

verdicts.note: Frost on the outdoor coil and reverse-cycle defrost both cut delivered heat, with the largest losses near freezing in humid air.

assertions.quote: That’s often electric resistive heating which will always work but needs a ton of energy to do so.

verdicts.note: Field studies in cold regions show strip heat use during cold snaps drives up winter electricity bills, especially with poor controls.

assertions.quote: even on today’s fossil-fired power grid, they’re a wiser use of limited resources and can help lower emissions.

verdicts.note: NREL and other modelling find air-source heat pumps lower emissions versus gas furnaces in most US regions on the current grid.

assertions.quote: all it really takes is a reversing valve and a few other particulars to make that happen, I see it as a no-brainer.

verdicts.note: A heat pump of the same capacity typically costs modestly more than an AC, and its heating displaces fuel or resistance heat.

assertions.quote: And the thing is, air conditioners ARE heat pumps.
some heat pumps like this are rated down to 20 below zero!

verdicts.note: NEEP-listed cold-climate models operate and deliver useful heat at -5°F to -22°F, with reduced capacity.

assertions.quote: that can put an untenable strain on the electric grid.

verdicts.note: Grid operators see winter peaks driven by resistance backup heat in cold snaps, though grid failures like Texas 2021 had mainly supply-side causes.
Full adoption would substantially raise peak electricity demand in many areas, particularly with lower-efficiency units with electric resistance backup and no envelope upgrades.
At 100% adoption, with supplemental heat modelled as resistance, cities covering 44% of the housing stock (mostly cold climates) see peak residential demand more than double.

The authors warn that if setback-driven auxiliary heat became widespread, winter electricity peaks could require major grid infrastructure, and they observed 10-15 kW resistance snapback after demand-response events; this is a projection, not measured grid strain.
